items.title: Load Balancers: The Traffic Cop That Saved the Internet
items.author: komal shehzadi
items.description:
Why one server was never going to be enough — and how the least glamorous box in your architecture quietly keeps everything boring.

The restaurant problem

Imagine you run a restaurant. You have one chef.

At 12 PM, five customers walk in. Easy.

At 1 PM, five hundred walk in.

Same chef.

Eventually, the kitchen catches fire. 🔥

That is more or less what happens when one server handles all of your traffic. And it is the exact problem the load balancer was built to solve. It looks at incoming requests and says:

“You go here. You go there. And you — please stop attacking Server 1.”

Load balancing didn’t appear because engineers thought round robin sounded cool. It appeared because of a very unglamorous fact:

One machine wasn’t enough anymore.

The 20-second version: a load balancer sits in front of your servers, picks one for every request, stops sending traffic to the ones that are dying, and lets you add or remove capacity without your users ever finding out. Everything below is the interesting detail.

🕰️ Before load balancers: one server, one prayer

The early web was beautifully simple:

User
  ↓
Web Server
  ↓
Database

One server. One app. One database. One hopefully-happy sysadmin.

Then websites got popular. More users meant more HTTP requests, more CPU, more memory, more database connections, more network traffic — until the server hit its ceiling.

At that point you had two options.

Option 1 — Buy a bigger machine (vertical scaling)

Small Server
     ↓
Bigger Server
     ↓
Even Bigger Server
     ↓
"Why does this server cost more than my house?"

It works. Until it doesn’t. There is always a physical ceiling, the price curve gets ugly long before you reach it, and upgrades usually mean downtime.

And when that one magnificent machine crashes, your entire application crashes with it.

Option 2 — Add more machines (horizontal scaling)

┌── Server 1
User ──┼── Server 2
       └── Server 3

Cheaper boxes, no hard ceiling, and no single machine whose death is fatal.

But now there is a new question: who decides which server gets the request?

Because you really don’t want users doing it themselves:

“Hmm… I’ll try Server 2 today.”

🚦 Enter the load balancer

A load balancer sits between your clients and your servers.

┌──► Server 1
                  │
Users ──► LB ─────┼──► Server 2
                  │
                  └──► Server 3

The client never learns which server answered. It talks to one address:

api.myapp.com

The load balancer works out the rest. That’s the whole abstraction, and it’s a good one:

One public endpoint. Many interchangeable backends.

🤔 What that actually buys you

1. Performance

Ten thousand requests per second can flatten a single server. Spread across five, it’s a Tuesday.

10,000 req/s
Server 1 → 2,000
Server 2 → 2,000
Server 3 → 2,000
Server 4 → 2,000
Server 5 → 2,000

2. Availability

Server 2 dies. 💥

The load balancer notices it is unhealthy and stops sending it traffic:

┌──► Server 1 ✅
              │
Users ──► LB ─┤    Server 2 ❌
              │
              └──► Server 3 ✅

Users may never notice. That’s high availability — and it’s the part people underestimate. Distributing load is nice; surviving a dead backend is why load balancers are non-negotiable in production.

Because in a distributed system, something will eventually break. Servers die. Networks vanish. Someone deploys at 4:59 PM on a Friday. You don’t design assuming failure won’t happen — you design so that failure is boring.

3. Scalability

Traffic is never flat:

Monday       → 10K requests
Tuesday      → 15K
Friday       → 50K
Black Friday → 2M 😵

You add servers behind the load balancer. The endpoint doesn’t change, the frontend doesn’t change, and your users don’t care. Capacity becomes an implementation detail.

4. Deployments that don’t hurt

Because the load balancer controls who receives traffic, you can pull one server out of rotation, upgrade it, and put it back — repeatedly.

Old version → 90%    →    Old version → 0%
New version → 10%         New version → 100%

That’s the machinery behind rolling deployments, canary releases and blue-green cutovers. All of it depends on something upstream being able to say “not you, not right now.”

5. A place to put cross-cutting concerns

TLS termination, HTTP/2, compression, access control, WAF integration, request logging. One well-configured chokepoint beats the same config copy-pasted onto twelve app servers.

🧠 How does it decide? The algorithms

There is no single magical algorithm. There are trade-offs.

Round Robin 🔄

Requests go out in sequence.

Request 1 → Server 1
Request 2 → Server 2
Request 3 → Server 3
Request 4 → Server 1

Basically: everyone gets a turn. Simple, predictable, stateless.

The catch: it assumes every server is equal and that every request costs the same. Neither is usually true. One /report/export can be worth ten thousand /health calls.

Server 1 → 64 CPU cores
Server 2 →  8 CPU cores

Handing both the same number of requests isn’t fairness. It’s arithmetic pretending to be fairness.

Weighted Round Robin ⚖️

Give each server a weight that reflects its capacity.

Server 1 → weight 5
Server 2 → weight 3
Server 3 → weight 2

More muscles, more boxes to carry. Useful for mixed hardware — and for deliberately trickling traffic to a new build.

Least Connections

Stop counting requests, start counting the ones still in flight.

Server 1 → 100 active
Server 2 →  40 active
Server 3 →  70 active
New request → Server 2

This is a much better default than round robin when request durations vary, because a struggling server naturally accumulates connections and stops being chosen.

Weighted Least Connections

Active connections and capacity. The sensible choice when your fleet isn’t uniform.

IP Hash and consistent hashing

Route by a hash of the client’s address:

hash(client_IP) % number_of_servers

Same client, same server — cheap session affinity with no state kept in the load balancer.

The catch is hiding in that % number_of_servers. Change the fleet size and most keys remap:

"I knew you, Server 2."
"Server 2 has left the chat."

Which is exactly why real systems use consistent hashing, where adding or removing a node only disturbs a small slice of the keyspace. Same idea, far less collateral damage — and the reason it’s also the standard trick for sharding a cache.

Least Response Time ⚡

Some load balancers factor in observed latency:

Server 1 →  20ms
Server 2 → 100ms
Server 3 →  35ms

Because the question isn’t only “where can I send this?” It’s “where can I send this and get a fast answer?”

Worth knowing: modern proxies often prefer power of two choices — sample two random backends, send the request to the less busy one. Nearly as good as inspecting every server, without the cost, and without everyone piling onto whichever backend currently looks best.

Honestly? For most applications the algorithm matters far less than the health checks. Round robin with good health checking beats least-response-time with bad health checking every single time.

🩺 Health checks: the unsung hero

Distributing traffic is only half the job. The load balancer also has to answer: is this server actually alive?

So it asks, on a schedule:

GET /health  →  200 OK     ✅ keep sending traffic
GET /health  →  500        ❌ pull from rotation
GET /health  →  timeout    ❌ pull from rotation

Three things worth getting right.

Active vs passive. Active checks poll an endpoint. Passive checks watch real traffic and eject a backend after N consecutive errors. Good setups do both — live traffic notices problems your synthetic probe never will.

Shallow vs deep. A /health that returns 200 OK unconditionally is decoration. One that verifies the database connection tells you something real — but if every instance shares that database, one database blip can mark your entire fleet unhealthy at once. The usual answer is two endpoints: a shallow liveness check for the load balancer, a deeper readiness check for orchestration.

Connection draining. When you remove a server, in-flight requests should finish before the process dies. Otherwise every deploy quietly serves a handful of 502s and everybody blames the network.

Because the rule is simple:

A dead server should not receive live traffic.

Obvious, isn’t it. And yet production systems find remarkably creative ways to disagree.

🍪 Sticky sessions (and why you probably don’t want them)

Say your app keeps session data in server memory.

Login     → LB → Server 1     (session lives here)
Next call → LB → Server 2     "…who are you?"

The user appears logged out. Rude.

The quick fix is sticky sessions: the load balancer pins each client to one backend, usually with a cookie of its own.

User A → Server 1
User B → Server 2
User C → Server 3

It works. It also quietly costs you:

  • the pinned server dies, and those users lose their sessions anyway
  • load stops being balanced — one unlucky server collects all the heavy users
  • autoscaling gets awkward, because fresh instances start out with nobody on them

The better architectural answer is to stop making servers special:

Redis  ·  Database  ·  Distributed cache

Put shared state there and any server can serve any request. That’s the entire point of stateless application servers — stickiness becomes an optimization instead of a load-bearing dependency.

🌐 Layer 4 vs Layer 7

Layer 4 — transport level

Works with TCP and UDP. It cares about:

IP  ·  Port  ·  Protocol  ·  Connection

It doesn’t read your HTTP request; it shuttles bytes between two sockets.

Client ──► TCP :443 ──► LB ──► Server

Fast, cheap, protocol-agnostic. Great for databases, gRPC streams, raw TCP, and anything where you want the payload left alone — including TLS you’d rather terminate on the backend.

Layer 7 — application level

Now it speaks HTTP, and can inspect the URL, method, headers, cookies and host:

/api/users/*   →  User Service
/api/orders/*  →  Order Service
/images/*      →  Image Server

That is not traffic distribution any more. That’s application-aware routing: path-based routing, header-based canaries, retries on idempotent methods, per-route timeouts, response caching, TLS termination.

The cost is real work per request — parsing, buffering, one more hop that can add latency, and one more place that can rewrite your headers in surprising ways.

Rule of thumb: Layer 4 when you want speed and transparency. Layer 7 when you want intelligence.

🏗️ In a microservice world

┌──► User Service
                     │
                     ├──► Order Service
Client ──► LB (L7) ──┤
                     ├──► Payment Service
                     │
                     └──► Notification Service

Route by path and you have a single front door for a dozen services:

/api/users     →  User Service
/api/orders    →  Order Service
/api/payments  →  Payment Service

At which point your load balancer starts to look suspiciously like an API gateway. Which raises a fair question.

🆚 Load balancer vs API gateway vs reverse proxy

They overlap constantly and the names get used loosely. The useful distinction is primary job.

A load balancer answers one question: where should this request go?

Load Balancer
    ↓
Traffic distribution + health + failover

An API gateway is a policy layer that happens to route:

API Gateway
    ↓
Routing
+ Authentication / authorization
+ Rate limiting and quotas
+ Request/response transformation
+ API composition and versioning
+ Per-consumer logging and analytics

A reverse proxy is the broader category both of them live inside: anything that accepts client requests on behalf of backends. TLS termination, caching, compression, header rewriting, routing — a load balancer is a reverse proxy with opinions about which backend.

This is why NGINX or Envoy can be all three depending on the config file. The label follows the job, not the binary.

🆚 The alternatives

A front-door load balancer isn’t the only way to spread traffic.

DNS load balancing

Return different addresses for the same name:

api.example.com  →  10.0.0.1
                 →  10.0.0.2
                 →  10.0.0.3

Dead simple, works across regions, no extra hop. But DNS was never designed to be a control plane: resolvers and clients cache aggressively, TTLs get ignored, and plain DNS round robin knows nothing about health. Great for coarse geographic distribution; poor at reacting to a server that died forty seconds ago.

Client-side load balancing (service discovery)

Let the caller choose. Services register with a discovery system, clients fetch the healthy instance list and pick for themselves.

Order Service
      ↓
Service Discovery
      ↓
Instance A · Instance B · Instance C

No extra network hop and no middle box to keep alive — at the price of putting that logic in every client, in every language you use.

Service mesh

The same idea, refactored: every service gets a sidecar proxy, and the mesh handles routing, retries, load balancing, mTLS, timeouts and observability uniformly.

Service ──► Sidecar ──► Sidecar ──► Service

Extremely powerful. Also the point at which your architecture diagram starts to look like someone spilled spaghetti on a whiteboard, and your latency budget picks up two extra hops.

🧩 Modern load balancing is boringly good

That’s a compliment.

Internet
                 ↓
       Cloud Load Balancer
                 ↓
       ┌─────────┼─────────┐
       ↓         ↓         ↓
    Instance  Instance  Instance
       1         2         3

Pair it with autoscaling and capacity follows demand:

Traffic up    →  3 servers → 6 servers
Traffic down  →  6 servers → 3 servers

The load balancer keeps distributing, the health checks keep pruning, and the endpoint never changes. A managed cloud load balancer is also horizontally scaled and multi-zone by default — which matters, for the reason below.

⚠️ Where it bites

Every component you add is a component you now have to operate. The things that will eventually demand your attention:

The load balancer becomes the single point of failure. If your diagram is:

Users ──► ONE Load Balancer ──► Many Servers

…then you have carefully distributed your servers and invented one new thing that can take the whole site down. 😂 The fix is redundancy at that layer too: an active-passive pair sharing a virtual IP, anycast, multiple zones — or a managed load balancer, where it’s someone else’s job.

Retry storms. The load balancer retries, the client retries, the SDK retries. A backend that is merely slow receives three times the traffic and becomes a backend that is dead. Use retry budgets, jittered backoff and circuit breakers.

Timeout mismatches. A load balancer idle timeout shorter than your backend’s keep-alive is the classic source of mysterious intermittent 502s. Keep the backend’s timeout longer than the proxy’s.

Health checks that lie. Too shallow and you route to broken servers. Too deep and one shared dependency ejects your entire fleet at once.

The lost client IP. Behind a proxy, every request appears to come from the load balancer. If you rate-limit or geolocate, you need X-Forwarded-For — and you need to trust only the hops you actually control.

None of this is a reason to skip the load balancer. It’s just the bill.

🧠 The bigger picture

The path most systems walk:

Single Server
     ↓
Vertical Scaling
     ↓
Multiple Servers
     ↓
Load Balancer
     ↓
Auto Scaling
     ↓
Microservices
     ↓
API Gateway / Service Mesh
     ↓
Highly Distributed Systems

The interesting part isn’t the load balancer. It’s the question underneath it:

How do we keep serving users while demand grows and individual components fail?

Distributed systems have been answering that one for decades. The load balancer was just the first honest answer.

🎯 Final takeaway

A load balancer is a traffic manager for your application. It sits between clients and backends and decides where each request goes.

It exists because a single server eventually becomes a bottleneck, and because betting your product on one machine is a genuinely terrifying way to live.

From round robin to Layer 7 routing, health checks, autoscaling, gateways, discovery and meshes — the core idea hasn’t moved:

LOAD BALANCER
                       ↓
             "Who can handle this?"
                       ↓
          ┌────────────┼────────────┐
          ↓            ↓            ↓
       Server 1     Server 2     Server 3
          ✅           ✅           ❌

And that’s the beauty of good infrastructure: when it’s working, nobody knows it’s there.

Your users click a button, and your system quietly decides who should deal with it.

No drama. No melted server. No “please try again later.”

Just traffic going where it should. 🚦

That’s a load balancer.

Best,

Komal

A load balancer is a traffic manager for your application. It sits between clients and backends and decides where each request goes.

                       ↓

And that’s the beauty of good infrastructure: when it’s working, nobody knows it’s there.

Your users click a button, and your system quietly decides who should deal with it.

No drama. No melted server. No “please try again later.”

Just traffic going where it should. 🚦

That’s a load balancer.

items.description:
Your app works beautifully.

Then users arrive.

Suddenly, the server is sweating, the database is crying, and someone in Slack types:

“Can we just increase the instance size?”

Welcome to scaling. 😄

Scaling is simply the art of making your system handle more work without falling apart.

And when it comes to scaling, there are two classic strategies:

  • Vertical scaling — make one machine bigger.
  • Horizontal scaling — add more machines.

Both work. Both have limits. And knowing when to use which one is a big part of designing systems that survive success.

🏗️ First: What Does “Scaling” Actually Mean?

Imagine you run a coffee shop.

At 9 AM, there are 10 customers.

Easy.

At 12 PM, there are 500 customers.

Now your single barista is making coffee like their life depends on it.

You have two options:

Option 1: Give the barista superpowers

Hire a faster barista, give them a bigger counter, better equipment, and a larger coffee machine.

That’s vertical scaling.

Option 2: Hire more baristas

Keep the same setup, but add more people making coffee.

That’s horizontal scaling.

Same problem.

Different strategy.

📈 Vertical Scaling

Vertical scaling, also called scaling up, means increasing the resources of an existing machine.

For example:

Before:
4 CPU
16 GB RAM
500 GB Storage
        ↓ SCALE UP
After:
16 CPU
64 GB RAM
2 TB Storage

You didn’t add another server.

You made the existing server stronger.

In cloud terms

You might go from:

AWS t3.medium
        ↓
AWS t3.2xlarge

or increase CPU/RAM on your VM or database instance.

It’s basically:

“This machine isn’t powerful enough. Give it more horsepower.”

🟢 Why Vertical Scaling Is Attractive

Vertical scaling is wonderfully simple.

You don’t necessarily need to redesign your application.

Your architecture can remain:

┌─────────────┐
Users ──────►│ Application │
             │   Server    │
             └──────┬──────┘
                    │
                    ▼
                Database

Make the application server bigger.

Done.

At least for a while.

Benefits

1. Simple

You don’t have to worry about distributing traffic across multiple application instances.

2. Less architectural complexity

No load balancing, service discovery, distributed coordination, etc.

3. Often easier for databases

Some databases benefit significantly from more CPU, RAM, and faster storage.

4. Great for early-stage systems

If you’re serving 500 users, you probably don’t need a 47-node Kubernetes cluster.

Please don’t become that person. 😄

🔴 The Problem With Vertical Scaling

Eventually, you hit a wall.

There is only so much CPU, RAM, disk, and network bandwidth you can put into one machine.

You can’t infinitely scale a server.

At some point:

4 CPU
 ↓
8 CPU
 ↓
16 CPU
 ↓
32 CPU
 ↓
64 CPU
 ↓
💸💸💸

And the next upgrade might be disproportionately expensive.

There is another problem:

The Single Machine Is Still a Single Point of Failure

If your entire application lives on one server:

Users
               │
               ▼
        ┌─────────────┐
        │ ONE SERVER  │
        └─────────────┘
               💥

Server goes down?

Your application goes down.

Congratulations.

You’ve horizontally scaled your downtime. 😅

🚀 Horizontal Scaling

Horizontal scaling, also called scaling out, means adding more machines or application instances.

Instead of making one server enormous:

Users
               │
               ▼
        ┌─────────────┐
        │   Server    │
        └─────────────┘

You add more:

Users
               │
               ▼
        ┌─────────────┐
        │Load Balancer│
        └──────┬──────┘
          ┌───┼───┐
          ▼   ▼   ▼
        ┌───┐┌───┐┌───┐
        │ A ││ B ││ C │
        └───┘└───┘└───┘

Now traffic can be distributed across multiple instances.

If 1,000 requests arrive:

Server A → 333
Server B → 333
Server C → 334

More servers.

More capacity.

More resilience.

🟢 Why Horizontal Scaling Is Powerful

1. More capacity

Need more processing power?

Add instances.

3 servers
   ↓
6 servers
   ↓
12 servers

You can keep expanding as demand increases.

2. Better availability

If one instance crashes:

Server A 💥
Server B ✅
Server C ✅

Users can continue using the application.

3. Elasticity

Cloud environments make this particularly powerful.

During normal traffic:

5 instances

During Black Friday:

50 instances

After Black Friday:

5 instances

Your infrastructure can scale with demand.

And unlike your office printer, you don’t need to physically buy anything. 😄

⚠️ But Horizontal Scaling Has a Catch

You just made your architecture more complicated.

Your application now needs to behave correctly when multiple instances are running simultaneously.

And this introduces one of the most important concepts in scalable architecture:

Statelessness

Imagine a user logs in.

Their session is stored in memory on Server A:

User
 │
 ▼
Server A
 │
 └── Session = "logged in"

Next request goes to Server B:

User
 │
 ▼
Server B
 │
 └── "Who are you?"

Oops.

This is why scalable applications typically avoid keeping important user state only in local memory.

Instead, state might live in something shared:

┌─────────────┐
             │Load Balancer│
             └──────┬──────┘
                    │
          ┌─────────┼─────────┐
          ▼         ▼         ▼
       Server A  Server B  Server C
          │         │         │
          └─────────┼─────────┘
                    ▼
                  Redis
                    │
                    ▼
                Database

Now any application instance can access the necessary state.

⚔️ Vertical vs. Horizontal

Here’s the quick comparison:

| **Vertical Scaling**        | **Horizontal Scaling**            |
| --------------------------- | --------------------------------- |
| Bigger machine              | More machines                     |
| Lower complexity            | Higher complexity                 |
| Limited by hardware         | Can scale across many machines    |
| Usually easier to implement | Requires distributed architecture |
| Limited fault tolerance     | Better fault tolerance            |
| Great for simple workloads  | Great for large-scale systems     |
| Example: 16 GB → 64 GB RAM  | Example: 1 server → 10 servers    |

🧠 So Which One Should You Choose?

The answer isn’t:

“Horizontal scaling is always better.”

That’s another classic engineering trap.

The real answer is:

Scale according to the bottleneck.

Suppose your application has:

API Servers
     │
     ▼
   Redis
     │
     ▼
 Database

You might horizontally scale your API:

API × 20

But if your database can only handle:

Database → 5,000 queries/sec

and those 20 servers generate:

Database → 50,000 queries/sec

Congratulations.

You just created a much faster way to destroy your database.

Scaling one layer doesn’t automatically scale the entire system.

🔥 The Real World Usually Uses Both

Modern architectures rarely choose only vertical or horizontal scaling.

They combine them.

For example:

Users
                   │
                   ▼
             Load Balancer
                   │
       ┌───────────┼───────────┐
       ▼           ▼           ▼
    API #1      API #2      API #3
       │           │           │
       └───────────┼───────────┘
                   ▼
                 Redis
                   │
                   ▼
             Database Cluster

You might:

  • Horizontally scale API servers.
  • Vertically scale individual API instances.
  • Add database replicas.
  • Increase database resources.
  • Use caching.
  • Introduce queues.
  • Partition large datasets.

Because real systems aren’t Lego bricks where one scaling strategy magically fixes everything.

📦 Don’t Forget the Database

Here’s where scaling gets interesting.

Application servers are often relatively easy to scale horizontally:

API × 2
API × 4
API × 8
API × 16

Databases are harder.

Why?

Because application servers can often be stateless.

Databases contain state.

And state is expensive.

You can’t simply say:

“Database is slow. Let’s create 100 copies.”

Well… you can.

Your database will just look at you differently afterward.

Database scaling might involve:

Read replicas

Database
                   │
          ┌────────┼────────┐
          ▼        ▼        ▼
       Replica   Replica   Replica

Reads can be distributed across replicas while writes go to the primary.

Sharding

Split data across multiple databases:

Users A–F → DB 1
Users G–M → DB 2
Users N–S → DB 3
Users T–Z → DB 4

Now the workload is distributed.

But you’ve also entered the wonderful world of distributed systems.

Bring coffee.

🧩 Scaling Isn’t Just About Servers

This is the part people sometimes miss.

You can have 100 servers and still have a slow application.

Why?

Because the bottleneck might be:

  • Database queries
  • Network latency
  • Disk I/O
  • Lock contention
  • External APIs
  • Memory leaks
  • Poor algorithms
  • Excessive logging
  • Synchronous processing
  • Large payloads
  • Inefficient queries

Sometimes the best scaling strategy isn’t:

“Add another server.”

It’s:

“Stop doing 47 unnecessary database queries.”

A single optimized query can sometimes beat an entire fleet of servers.

🎯 A Simple Mental Model

Think about scaling like a restaurant.

Vertical scaling

Make one restaurant bigger.

🍽️
100 seats
 ↓
500 seats

Horizontal scaling

Open more restaurants.

🍽️   🍽️   🍽️   🍽️

Caching

Prepare popular dishes in advance.

🔥 Popular dish → Ready immediately

Load balancing

Send customers to restaurants with available tables.

Customer
   ↓
"Restaurant #2 has space."

Database sharding

Different restaurants keep different inventories.

And suddenly your software architecture starts looking suspiciously like a food business.

🚦 When Should You Scale?

Don’t scale because someone said:

“We’re going to have millions of users someday.”

Scale when you have evidence.

Monitor things like:

  • CPU utilization
  • Memory usage
  • Request latency
  • Requests per second
  • Error rates
  • Database CPU
  • Database connections
  • Queue depth
  • Cache hit rate
  • Disk I/O

For example:

CPU:        92%  🚨
Latency:    2.8s 🚨
Errors:     4.2% 🚨
Traffic:    +180%

That’s a pretty good conversation starter.

But:

CPU:        18%
Latency:    80ms
Errors:     0.01%

Maybe leave the infrastructure alone.

Your cloud bill will thank you.

🏁 The Bottom Line

Vertical scaling asks:

“How can I make this machine more powerful?”

Horizontal scaling asks:

“How can I make the workload run across more machines?”

Vertical scaling is simple and extremely useful.

Horizontal scaling is more complex, but gives you greater capacity, elasticity, and resilience.

And the best production systems usually don’t pick sides.

They use the right strategy at the right layer.

Because scaling isn’t really about adding servers.

It’s about removing bottlenecks while keeping the system reliable, predictable, and affordable.

And that’s the real engineering challenge.

Anyone can throw more servers at a problem.

The fun part is figuring out which problem actually needs more servers. 🚀

Best,

Komal

items.description:
The request succeeded, the dashboards are green, and the user still can’t submit the form. Grafana Faro is the flight recorder that shows you what your server never saw.

Every frontend engineer knows this ticket. “It doesn’t work.” No steps, no browser, no timestamp, one blurry screenshot of a half-rendered form. You open the same page, click the same button, and it works perfectly — nine times in a row.

So you go to the logs. The API returned 200. The gateway is calm. Every dashboard is green. And that is precisely the problem: your server logs end at the network boundary, and the bug lives on the far side of it, inside a browser you will never touch, running an extension you have never heard of, on a connection that dropped for 400 milliseconds at exactly the wrong moment.

  • Web vitals — LCP, CLS, INP and friends, from real users on real devices, not a lab run.
  • Route changes — navigation inside a single-page app, so you can see the path someone actually walked.
  • Session identity — a session id, a browser/OS fingerprint, your app name, environment and release, stamped on everything.

1. What led up to it

2. How bad it is

3. Whether you caused it

});

Reading it back

Signals land in Loki, and you query them with LogQL: pick a stream by labels, parse the line, then filter on any field. The whole language reduces to a handful of moves in practice.

# everything the frontend sent, in prod
{app="checkout-web", env="prod"}
# only the failures
{app="checkout-web", env="prod"} | logfmt | level = "error"
# one session, in order — the story of a single visit
{app="checkout-web"} | logfmt | session_id = "a41f9c…"
# did the new release make it worse?
sum by (version) (
  count_over_time({app="checkout-web"} | logfmt | level = "error" [5m])
)

Two habits keep this fast. Put low-cardinality things in labels (app, environment, kind) and high-cardinality things in the line (session ids, user ids, request ids) — a label per user id is the classic way to bring an index to its knees. And keep one naming convention: mixed casing across dashboards costs more afternoons than it has any right to.

The honest advantages

  • One pane of glass. Browser errors sit beside API metrics and infrastructure logs, so you stop arguing across tool boundaries about whose fault it is.
  • Open source, no lock-in. Faro is Apache-licensed and OpenTelemetry-friendly. Your data lands in stores you control, in formats you can leave with.
  • Cheap storage model. Loki indexes labels, not full text. Keeping a lot of frontend logs is unusually affordable compared with search-engine-backed alternatives.
  • Real users, real devices. Synthetic checks pass on your laptop. Field data is the only thing that tells you about the mid-range Android on hotel wifi.
  • It composes. Same collector, same query language, same dashboards, same alerting as the rest of the stack. New signal, not a new system.

And the bill

Anything that claims no trade-offs is selling something. These are the ones worth knowing before you commit:

  • Beacons get blocked. Ad blockers, privacy extensions and strict corporate proxies quietly drop telemetry requests. Your data is a sample of reality, not reality.
  • Minified stacks are useless without source maps. Uploading and managing them is real, ongoing work, and it is the step teams most often skip and then regret.
  • You own the plumbing. Self-hosting means somebody keeps the collector and Loki healthy, retention tuned and dashboards from rotting. That is a genuine cost, just not a licence fee.
  • PII is your problem. Nothing stops you shipping a token, an OTP, a national id or a full request body straight into a log store. Redact at the source, and treat “log the whole payload” as a decision, not a default.
  • Noise wins if you let it. Browser extensions and third-party scripts throw errors you can never fix. Without a deliberate ignore list, the signal drowns and people stop looking — which is the real failure mode.
  • No session replay. Faro shows you signals, not a video. If your team wants to watch the user’s screen, that is a different category of tool.

The alternatives, fairly

Faro is the natural pick when you already live in Grafana. If you don’t, some of these are a better answer, and pretending otherwise wastes everyone’s quarter.

Grafana Faro — open source, self-hosted or Grafana Cloud. Strongest at: unifying browser signals with an existing Grafana/Loki stack, at low storage cost. The catch: you assemble and operate the pipeline; no replay; the smallest ecosystem of the group.

Sentry — open source core, or SaaS. Strongest at: error triage — grouping, ownership, release health, suspect commits. The benchmark of the genre. The catch: error-first by design; broad telemetry and long retention get expensive.

Datadog RUM — SaaS. Strongest at: end-to-end correlation from click to backend span, with session replay included. The catch: premium pricing and deep lock-in; overkill unless you are already all-in on Datadog.

Elastic APM RUM — self-hosted or Elastic Cloud. Strongest at: full-text search over telemetry when an ELK stack already exists. The catch: heavier to run; index cost climbs fast with volume.

OpenTelemetry JS — open standard, self-assembled. Strongest at: maximum portability and vendor neutrality — one standard, any backend. The catch: a toolkit, not a product. Browser support lags the server story; you build the rest.

LogRocket / FullStory — SaaS. Strongest at: watching exactly what the user saw. Unbeatable for “cannot reproduce” UX bugs. The catch: replay carries the heaviest privacy burden of anything here; weaker as an engineering log.

PostHog — open source or SaaS. Strongest at: product analytics, funnels and feature flags sharing one event stream with error tracking. The catch: analytics-shaped first; less depth for pure debugging.

  2. Want the best error triage with no plumbing? Sentry, and stop researching.
  3. Losing days to UX bugs you cannot reproduce? Buy replay, then negotiate the privacy review early rather than late.
  4. Betting on portability above all? OpenTelemetry, with clear eyes about how much you will assemble yourself.

And a real option people forget: pick one and instrument it properly. A single tool with stable event names, redaction and a dashboard somebody actually opens beats three half-configured ones every single time.

The goal was never prettier graphs. It is deleting the sentence “I cannot reproduce it” from your vocabulary — and replacing it with a query you can run before the reporter has finished typing.

items.title: HTTP QUERY: The Missing Middle Between GET and POST
items.author: komal shehzadi
items.description:
For years, HTTP developers have lived with a slightly awkward choice:

GET when you want to retrieve data.

POST when you need to send a body.

Simple enough — until your “GET” query becomes a 2,000-line JSON object.

Then things get interesting.

In June 2026, the IETF published RFC 10008, formally defining a new HTTP method called QUERY. Its goal is surprisingly elegant:

Give us a way to perform a safe, idempotent query using a request body.

In other words, QUERY sits in the gap between GET and POST.

The Problem QUERY Is Trying to Solve

Consider a simple API:

GET /products?category=laptop&brand=dell&minPrice=1000

Perfect.

GET was made for this kind of thing.

But now imagine an enterprise search API:

{
  "filters": {
    "categories": ["laptop", "monitor"],
    "brands": ["Dell", "Lenovo", "Apple"],
    "price": {
      "min": 1000,
      "max": 5000
    },
    "availability": true
  },
  "sorting": [
    {
      "field": "price",
      "direction": "ascending"
    }
  ],
  "pagination": {
    "page": 4,
    "pageSize": 100
  }
}

Trying to squeeze this into a URL is… let’s just say the URL has started making career decisions of its own.

You could encode everything:

GET /products?categories=laptop,monitor&brands=Dell,Lenovo,Apple&minPrice=1000&maxPrice=5000&availability=true&sort=price:asc&page=4&pageSize=100

But as queries become more complex, URLs become harder to construct, encode, read, log, maintain, and sometimes even transport reliably.

The HTTP specification itself identifies several problems with putting large or complex query inputs into the URI, including URI size constraints, encoding overhead, and the fact that request URIs are more likely to be logged or bookmarked than request content.

So developers historically found another solution.

“Fine, Let’s Just Use POST.”

And that’s exactly what many APIs do.

POST /products/search
Content-Type: application/json
{
  "filters": {
    "categories": ["laptop", "monitor"],
    "brands": ["Dell", "Lenovo"]
  },
  "pagination": {
    "page": 4,
    "pageSize": 100
  }
}

From a practical API-development perspective, this works beautifully.

The problem isn’t that POST can’t do this.

The problem is semantics.

When another developer sees:

POST /products/search

they can’t infer from the HTTP method alone whether this operation:

  • creates something,
  • modifies something,
  • triggers an action,
  • performs a search,
  • or does something else entirely.

They have to understand the application’s API contract.

HTTP already has a concept for this:

safe operations.

And that’s where QUERY comes in.

Enter QUERY

With QUERY, the same operation can become:

QUERY /products
Content-Type: application/json
{
  "filters": {
    "categories": ["laptop", "monitor"],
    "brands": ["Dell", "Lenovo"]
  },
  "pagination": {
    "page": 4,
    "pageSize": 100
  }
}

Now the HTTP method itself communicates something important:

“I’m querying this resource, and I’m not asking you to change its state.”

According to RFC 10008, QUERY is explicitly defined as both safe and idempotent. Its request content describes how the target resource should process the query.

That’s the key idea.

But Wait… Can’t GET Have a Body?

This is probably the first question any experienced backend developer will ask.

And it’s a fair one.

You might have seen this:

GET /products
Content-Type: application/json
{
  "category": "laptop",
  "minPrice": 1000
}

Some HTTP clients and servers will technically let you send this.

But here’s the important distinction:

GET request content has no defined semantics.

RFC 10008 explicitly contrasts this with QUERY: QUERY expects request content, and the content plus its media type defines the query.

So the problem isn’t simply:

“Can bytes physically be sent after a GET request?”

They can.

The real question is:

“Does HTTP define those bytes as the input to the GET operation?”

For GET, the answer is effectively no.

For QUERY, the answer is yes.

That distinction matters enormously when intermediaries, caches, proxies, frameworks, and other HTTP infrastructure are involved.

GET vs QUERY vs POST

Here’s the easiest mental model:

Feature              | GET                    | QUERY                         | POST
---------------------|------------------------|-------------------------------|----------------------------
Primary purpose      | Retrieve a resource    | Execute a safe, complex query | Submit/process data
Request body         | No defined semantics   | Designed for a request body   | Supported
Safe                 | Yes                    | Yes                           | Not necessarily
Idempotent           | Yes                    | Yes                           | Not necessarily
Complex query body   | Not defined            | Designed for it               | Common workaround
Parameters           | Usually in URL         | Can be in body                | Usually in body
Cacheability         | Well supported         | Defined as cacheable          | Limited
Typical use          | GET /users?id=123      | QUERY /users + JSON           | POST /users + JSON
State change         | No                     | No                            | Potentially
Best suited for      | Simple retrieval       | Complex read/search           | Create/update/actions

The IETF specification explicitly describes QUERY as a bridge between GET and POST: like POST, it carries the query input in request content; unlike POST, it is explicitly safe and idempotent.

The Three Methods in One Example

Imagine we’re building a customer search API.

GET

For simple queries:

GET /customers?country=Pakistan&status=active

This is clean, readable, bookmarkable and easy to cache.

Use GET.

POST

Now imagine the request performs an operation that can modify state:

POST /customers
Content-Type: application/json
{
  "name": "Komi",
  "country": "Pakistan"
}

We’re creating something.

Use POST.

QUERY

Now imagine we’re searching millions of customers using a sophisticated query:

QUERY /customers
Content-Type: application/json
{
  "filters": {
    "country": ["Pakistan", "UAE"],
    "status": ["active"],
    "age": {
      "min": 25,
      "max": 40
    }
  },
  "search": {
    "fields": ["name", "email", "company"],
    "text": "software engineer"
  },
  "sort": [
    {
      "field": "createdAt",
      "direction": "desc"
    }
  ]
}

We’re not creating or modifying customers.

We’re asking:

“Give me the result of this query.”

That’s precisely the territory QUERY is designed for.

The Really Important Part: Idempotency

There’s another reason QUERY is interesting.

Suppose a network connection drops after the server receives your request.

Can the client safely retry it?

With a safe, idempotent operation, that’s much easier to reason about.

QUERY is explicitly idempotent, meaning it can be repeated or automatically retried without expecting a partial state change to the target resource.

POST doesn’t give you that guarantee.

For example:

POST /payment

You definitely don’t want some infrastructure blindly deciding:

“Hmm, connection failed. Let’s try that payment again.”

💸💸💸

For QUERY:

QUERY /products

retrying the same read operation is fundamentally different because the method is defined as safe and idempotent.

What About Caching?

This is another interesting piece.

GET has always played nicely with HTTP caching.

For example:

GET /products?category=laptop

items.title: The Real AI Productivity Gain Isn’t Coding. It’s Root Cause Analysis.
items.author: komal shehzadi
items.description:
For the past several months, a big part of my work has been fixing bugs deep inside a large, mature enterprise application — years of history, layered abstractions, legacy decisions, and hundreds of business rules that quietly matter.

In systems like this, writing the fix is rarely the hard part.

Finding the root cause is.

A typical bug fix might end up being three lines of code sitting on top of three hours of investigation. The investigation is the job. And that’s exactly where having Claude as a pair-debugging partner has fundamentally changed how I work.

Root Cause Analysis Is a Search Problem

When something breaks in a mature codebase, the symptom is almost never where the cause lives.

A button stays disabled, but the real issue is a validator failing on a field three components away.

Data remains visible after a reset, but the actual bug is two state objects quietly drifting out of sync upstream.

A workflow crashes on the final step, but the root cause is a value that was never captured several screens earlier.

Root cause analysis is essentially a search problem. You’re searching across files, call chains, services, state transitions, business rules, and the gap between what the code says should happen and what actually happens at runtime.

The expensive part isn’t reading a file.

It’s holding twenty files in your head at once while maintaining a coherent mental model of the system.

That’s where Claude has been surprisingly valuable.

Following the Trail End-to-End

The biggest productivity boost comes from Claude’s ability to trace execution paths across large sections of a codebase and explain the flow in plain language.

Instead of manually jumping through definitions, handlers, models, services, and UI layers, I can ask:

“How does this value get from here to there?”

And Claude will often produce a detailed chain:

  • Which definition resolves to which handler
  • Where data is transformed
  • Which conditions affect execution
  • Where values are introduced, modified, or discarded
  • Which assumptions downstream code relies on

The value isn’t that it magically finds the bug.

The value is that it dramatically reduces the cost of understanding the system.

What used to take an hour of manually traversing code often takes minutes.

That means I can spend more time reasoning and less time navigating.

The Surprising Value of Being Wrong

One thing I’ve come to appreciate is that Claude is a tireless investigator.

It doesn’t get frustrated after the eighth pass through the same module.

It doesn’t mind exploring dead ends.

And sometimes its most valuable contribution is proving that my assumptions are wrong.

There have been plenty of situations where Claude traced the entire chain and concluded:

“Based on the code, this should be working.”

At first, that sounds unhelpful.

In reality, it’s often the breakthrough.

Because if the code says the feature should work and production says it doesn’t, then the real problem probably lives outside the assumptions we’re making.

Those contradictions frequently become the clues that lead to the actual root cause.

Hypotheses Are Cheap. Evidence Solves Cases.

The biggest lesson I’ve learned is this:

Claude is a fast investigator, not an oracle.

More than once, both Claude and I arrived at a confident explanation that turned out to be completely wrong.

The theories sounded reasonable.

The logic seemed airtight.

The bug wasn’t there.

What actually solved those cases was evidence.

A network payload.

A console log.

A screenshot.

A production trace.

A business rule that wasn’t documented anywhere.

The moment real evidence entered the conversation, the analysis sharpened dramatically and the correct explanation emerged.

The most effective RCA loop I’ve found looks like this:

  1. Claude maps the terrain.
  • Trace the execution path.
  • Surface potential failure points.
  • Explain why each suspect could be responsible.
  1. I provide ground truth.
  • Logs.
  • Payloads.
  • Screenshots.
  • Runtime observations.
  • Domain knowledge.
  1. We converge through elimination.
  • Discard plausible-but-wrong theories.
  • Challenge assumptions.
  • Continue until the code and evidence agree.

The skepticism is the feature, not the flaw.

Many of the best root causes I’ve found this year appeared only after throwing away the first explanation.

Why Experience Matters More, Not Less

There’s another aspect that doesn’t get discussed enough.

Claude becomes dramatically more useful when paired with strong engineering fundamentals.

The better you understand software architecture, state management, debugging techniques, design patterns, and business domains, the better questions you ask and the better you can evaluate the answers.

An experienced engineer can recognize:

  • Which execution paths are actually relevant
  • Which assumptions need validation
  • Which theories violate known system behavior
  • Which findings deserve deeper investigation

In other words, expertise acts as a multiplier.

Claude can traverse a codebase incredibly quickly, but knowing where to dig, what evidence matters, and when an explanation doesn’t quite add up still requires engineering judgment.

The strongest results come from combining both:

  • Human intuition and experience
  • AI-powered exploration and analysis

Neither is as effective alone as they are together.

The Real Takeaway

The promise everyone talks about is:

“AI writes your code.”

My experience has been different.

The real value is that Claude compresses the time between:

“Something is broken.”

and

“I understand exactly why.”

On large, complex, high-stakes systems, that compression is enormous.

It transforms debugging from hours of spelunking through layers of abstraction into a focused investigation where I spend my energy on judgment, trade-offs, risk assessment, and solution design instead of manually walking call graphs.

I’m still the engineer.

I still own every decision, every change, and every line that ships.

But my root cause analysis is faster, deeper, and more evidence-driven than it’s ever been because I have a tireless partner that can read, connect, and reason across a codebase at a speed that simply wasn’t possible before.

If you work on large, legacy, or highly complex systems, I’m curious:

How are you incorporating AI into your RCA process, and where has it genuinely helped — or failed — to uncover the truth?

Best,

Komal

items.title: RxJS in Angular (and the “Do I really need this?” Survival Guide)
items.author: komal shehzadi
items.description:
Let’s be honest for a second.

You open an Angular project…
You see .pipe(map(), switchMap(), catchError(), debounceTime())…
And suddenly you’re questioning your life choices.

Welcome to the world of RxJS 😄

But here’s the twist:
RxJS isn’t the villain. It’s just… a bit dramatic for simple problems.

So let’s break this down in a way that actually makes sense — and maybe even enjoy it a little.

🎭 RxJS: The Overachiever Friend

RxJS is like that one friend who:

  • Plans everything
  • Optimizes everything
  • Has a system for everything

And you’re just like:

“Bro I just wanted to fetch some data…”

What RxJS actually does:

It handles data over time (streams):

  • API responses
  • User typing
  • Button clicks
  • Live updates

It’s insanely powerful. But sometimes… unnecessarily powerful.

😵 When RxJS Feels Like Too Much

You:

“I just need to call an API.”

RxJS:

“Let’s create a stream, transform it, cancel it, retry it, merge it, debounce it…”

You:

“…never mind.”

🧩 Chill Alternatives (a.k.a. “Use This Instead Sometimes”)

🚀 1. Signals — The Cool New Kid

Angular basically said:

“Okay yeah… RxJS is a lot. Let’s relax.”

Enter Signals.

const count = signal(0);
count.set(1);

That’s it. No subscriptions. No pipes. No existential crisis.

Why Signals slap:

  • Super simple
  • Built for UI state
  • No memory leaks
  • Feels natural

👉 Perfect for:

  • Component state
  • UI updates
  • Derived values

Vibe check: Signals are RxJS after therapy.

🌐 2. Promises — The “Keep It Simple” Option

Sometimes you just want:

const data = await fetch('/api/data').then(r => r.json());

No streams. No operators. Just vibes.

Good for:

  • One-time API calls
  • Clean async/await flow

Not good for:

  • Real-time updates
  • Complex async logic

Vibe check: Promises are “I’ll deal with it once and move on.”

🧠 3. State Libraries — Let Someone Else Handle the Chaos

Big app? Things getting messy?

Bring in:

  • NgRx
  • NGXS
  • Akita

They still use RxJS… but behind the scenes like a responsible adult.

You just:

  • Dispatch actions
  • Select state
  • Stay sane

Vibe check: “I don’t want to manage this. You do it.”

🔄 4. Async Pipe — The Lazy Genius Move

Instead of this:

this.users$.subscribe(users => this.users = users);

Just do this:

<div *ngIf="users$ | async as users">
  {{ users.length }}
</div>

Angular handles everything.

You sip tea ☕.

Vibe check: Maximum output, minimum effort.

⚙️ 5. Event Emitters — Keep It Old School

@Output() clicked = new EventEmitter();

Simple. Clean. No overthinking.

Perfect for:

  • Parent ↔ child communication

Vibe check: “Why are we complicating this?”

⚖️ Real Talk: Can You Escape RxJS?

Short answer: Nope.

Long answer:

  • Angular uses RxJS internally
  • HttpClient? RxJS
  • Router? RxJS
  • Forms? RxJS

So even if you avoid it… it’s still there. Watching. Waiting. 😄

🧠 The Real Flex (What Actually Matters)

Senior dev energy is not:

“I know RxJS.”

It’s:

“I know when NOT to use RxJS.”

🎯 Quick Cheat Sheet

SituationWhat to UseUI stateSignals 🚀Simple API callPromise 🌐Complex async flowRxJS 🎭Template bindingAsync Pipe 🔄Large-scale stateNgRx / NGXS / Akita 🧠

💡 Final Thought

RxJS is like a Swiss Army knife.

Super powerful.
Super useful.
But you don’t use it to open a bag of chips.

Modern Angular gives you options — Signals, Promises, smarter patterns.

Use the right tool, and suddenly Angular feels… easy.

And honestly? That’s the real win.

items.title: From Bots to Bosses: Why Agentic AI Is Running the Future
items.author: komal shehzadi
items.description:
There was a time when AI politely waited for instructions — like that one intern who wouldn’t move unless you gave them a checklist, a pep talk, and probably coffee. Those days? Over. Welcome to the era of Agentic AI — where machines don’t just respond, they act.

So… What Is Agentic AI?

Agentic AI refers to systems that can make decisions, take initiative, and execute tasks autonomously — all while adapting to changing environments. Think less “calculator” and more “colleague who just handled three problems before you even noticed them.”

Instead of prompting AI step-by-step, you give it a goal:

“Plan my product launch,”
“Optimize this workflow,”
“Find the best solution to this problem.”

And it figures out the how — on its own.

The Shift: From Tools to Teammates

Traditional AI is like a super-smart tool. Agentic AI? It’s more like a proactive teammate.

Here’s the difference:

  • Old AI: “Tell me what to do next.”
  • Agentic AI: “I’ve already started, here’s the progress, and I fixed two issues along the way.”

It can:

  • Break down complex goals into actionable steps
  • Learn from feedback and refine its approach
  • Coordinate multiple tasks simultaneously
  • Even collaborate with other AI agents (yes, teamwork makes the dream work — even for machines)

Why Everyone’s Talking About It

Because this isn’t just an upgrade — it’s a paradigm shift.

🚀 1. Productivity on Steroids

Agentic AI doesn’t wait around. It identifies inefficiencies, optimizes workflows, and executes tasks — freeing humans to focus on strategy and creativity.

🧠 2. Smarter Decision-Making

These systems can process massive datasets, simulate outcomes, and choose optimal paths — faster than any human team.

🔄 3. Continuous Learning

They don’t just complete tasks — they improve with every iteration. Like a colleague who never forgets a lesson.

🌐 4. End-to-End Automation

From planning to execution, agentic AI can handle entire processes — not just fragments.

Real-World Vibes

Imagine this:

  • A startup founder wakes up to find their AI has already analyzed market trends, adjusted pricing, and scheduled investor meetings.
  • A developer assigns a bug fix, and the AI not only patches it — but tests, deploys, and monitors performance.
  • A parent juggling life gets help from an AI that anticipates needs — reminders, planning, even decision support.

It’s not sci-fi anymore. It’s quietly becoming… normal.

But Wait — Should We Be Nervous?

Short answer: a little cautious, a lot excited.

Agentic AI raises important questions:

  • Who’s accountable for decisions?
  • How do we ensure alignment with human values?
  • What happens when autonomy goes wrong?

The future isn’t about replacing humans — it’s about designing AI that augments us responsibly.

The Big Picture

Agentic AI marks the transition from:

“AI as a tool” → “AI as an autonomous problem-solver”

And that changes everything.

We’re moving toward a world where:

  • Work is more about direction than execution
  • Creativity and judgment become our biggest assets
  • Humans and AI collaborate in ways we’re just starting to imagine

Final Thought

If the last decade was about building smarter machines, this decade is about building independent thinkers (well… almost thinkers).

Agentic AI isn’t just the future — it’s already knocking on the door, probably with a fully optimized plan in hand.

And honestly? It might already have a backup plan too. 😉

Best,

Komal Shehzadi

items.title: Level Up Your React Game: Unleash the Power of Custom Hooks!
items.author: komal shehzadi
items.description:
Have you ever found yourself copy-pasting the same useEffect and useState logic across different components? We’ve all been there. It starts with a simple timer, and suddenly, your codebase is a "spaghetti" of redundant logic.

Enter Custom Hooks — the React developer’s secret weapon for writing clean, reusable, and professional code. Today, we’re going to take a messy situation and turn it into a masterpiece using a Stopwatch example.

The Problem: Logic Bloat 🍔

Imagine you need a stopwatch on your dedicated “Timer Page,” but you also want a small stopwatch widget on your “Dashboard.” If you write the setInterval logic in both places, you’re doubling your work and your bugs.

Professional React development is all about DRY (Don’t Repeat Yourself). We want to extract the behavior of the stopwatch so any component can just “plug it in” and work.

The Solution: Our Custom useStopwatch Hook 🛠️

Instead of trapping our logic inside a component, we package it into a neat function. This is our Engine.

Take a look at how we’ve abstracted the timing logic in stopWatch.tsx:

// hooks/stopWatch.tsx
'use client';
import { useState, useEffect } from "react";
export function useStopwatch() {
    const [time, setTime] = useState(0);
    const [isRunning, setIsRunning] = useState(false);
    useEffect(() => {
        let id: NodeJS.Timeout | null = null;
        if (isRunning) {
            id = setInterval(() => {
                setTime(prevTime => prevTime + 1);
            }, 1000);
        }
        return () => { if (id) clearInterval(id); };
    }, [isRunning]);

    const start = () => setIsRunning(true);
    const stop = () => setIsRunning(false);
    const reset = () => { setIsRunning(false); setTime(0); };
    const formatTime = () => {
        const minutes = Math.floor(time / 60);
        const seconds = time % 60;
        return `${String(minutes).padStart(2, '0')}:${String(seconds).padStart(2, '0')}`;
    };
    return { time, isRunning, start, stop, reset, formattedTime: formatTime() };
}

Why this is awesome:

  • Encapsulation: The component doesn’t need to know how setInterval works. It just asks for the formattedTime.
  • Clean Up: It handles its own garbage collection (clearing the interval) so you don’t get memory leaks.
  • Simplicity: It returns a simple API: start, stop, and reset.

Implementation: One Hook, Two Very Different Worlds 🌍

Because we built a Custom Hook, we can now use this logic in completely different UI layouts without rewriting a single line of math.

1. The Full-Screen Experience

In StopwatchPage.tsx, we use the hook to create a beautiful, centered standalone app.

export default function StopwatchPage() {
    const { formattedTime, isRunning, start, stop, reset } = useStopwatch();
    // ... just drop these into your Tailwind buttons!
}

2. The Integrated Dashboard

In the main page.tsx, we have a busy landing page with cards and buttons. We can drop the exact same stopwatch logic right into the middle of this complex layout.

export default function Home() {
  const { formattedTime, isRunning, start, stop, reset } = useStopwatch();
  // Now we have a stopwatch living alongside our cards!

return (
    <div className="space-y-10">
      {/* Stopwatch Section */}
      <section className="rounded-xl border border-slate-200 bg-white p-6 shadow-sm">
        <h2 className="text-xl font-semibold text-slate-900 mb-4">
          {"Stopwatch"}
        </h2>
        <div className="flex items-center gap-4">
          <div className="text-4xl font-mono font-bold text-slate-900 tabular-nums">
            {formattedTime}
          </div>
          <div className="flex gap-2">
            {!isRunning ? (
              <button
                onClick={start}
                className="px-4 py-2 bg-emerald-600 text-white rounded-lg hover:bg-emerald-700 transition-colors font-medium"
              >
               {"Start"}
              </button>
            ) : (
              <button
                onClick={stop}
                className="px-4 py-2 bg-red-600 text-white rounded-lg hover:bg-red-700 transition-colors font-medium"
              >
                {"Stop"}
              </button>
            )}
            <button
              onClick={reset}
              className="px-4 py-2 bg-slate-600 text-white rounded-lg hover:bg-slate-700 transition-colors font-medium"
            >
              {"Reset"}
            </button>
          </div>
        </div>
      </section>
</div>

}

Pro-Tips for Your Custom Hooks 💡

  • Always Start with “use”: React’s linter looks for the use prefix (like useStopwatch) to ensure you're following the Rules of Hooks.
  • Keep it Focused: A hook should do one thing well. Don’t make a useUserAndStopwatchAndTheme hook!
  • Return what you need: You can return arrays (like useState) or objects (like our useStopwatch). Objects are usually better when you have more than two return values!

Final Thoughts 🏁

Custom hooks turn you from a “coder” into an “architect.” They make your components purely about the look (UI), while your hooks handle the brain (Logic).

Next time you find yourself writing a useEffect that looks familiar, ask yourself: "Should this be a Custom Hook?" The answer is usually a resounding YES.

Happy coding! 🚀

Komal

    const formatTime = () => {
        const minutes = Math.floor(time / 60);
        const seconds = time % 60;
        return `${String(minutes).padStart(2, '0')}:${String(seconds).padStart(2, '0')}`;
    };
    return { time, isRunning, start, stop, reset, formattedTime: formatTime() };
}

Why this is awesome:

  • Encapsulation: The component doesn’t need to know how setInterval works. It just asks for the formattedTime.
  • Clean Up: It handles its own garbage collection (clearing the interval) so you don’t get memory leaks.
  • Simplicity: It returns a simple API: start, stop, and reset.

Implementation: One Hook, Two Very Different Worlds 🌍

Because we built a Custom Hook, we can now use this logic in completely different UI layouts without rewriting a single line of math.

1. The Full-Screen Experience

In StopwatchPage.tsx, we use the hook to create a beautiful, centered standalone app.

export default function StopwatchPage() {
    const { formattedTime, isRunning, start, stop, reset } = useStopwatch();
    // ... just drop these into your Tailwind buttons!
}

2. The Integrated Dashboard

In the main page.tsx, we have a busy landing page with cards and buttons. We can drop the exact same stopwatch logic right into the middle of this complex layout.

export default function Home() {
  const { formattedTime, isRunning, start, stop, reset } = useStopwatch();
  // Now we have a stopwatch living alongside our cards!

return (
    <div className="space-y-10">
      {/* Stopwatch Section */}
      <section className="rounded-xl border border-slate-200 bg-white p-6 shadow-sm">
        <h2 className="text-xl font-semibold text-slate-900 mb-4">
          {"Stopwatch"}
        </h2>
        <div className="flex items-center gap-4">
          <div className="text-4xl font-mono font-bold text-slate-900 tabular-nums">
            {formattedTime}
          </div>
          <div className="flex gap-2">
            {!isRunning ? (
              <button
                onClick={start}
                className="px-4 py-2 bg-emerald-600 text-white rounded-lg hover:bg-emerald-700 transition-colors font-medium"
              >
               {"Start"}
              </button>
            ) : (
              <button
                onClick={stop}
                className="px-4 py-2 bg-red-600 text-white rounded-lg hover:bg-red-700 transition-colors font-medium"
              >
                {"Stop"}
              </button>
            )}
            <button
              onClick={reset}
              className="px-4 py-2 bg-slate-600 text-white rounded-lg hover:bg-slate-700 transition-colors font-medium"
            >
              {"Reset"}
            </button>
          </div>
        </div>
      </section>
</div>

}

Pro-Tips for Your Custom Hooks 💡

  • Always Start with “use”: React’s linter looks for the use prefix (like useStopwatch) to ensure you're following the Rules of Hooks.
  • Keep it Focused: A hook should do one thing well. Don’t make a useUserAndStopwatchAndTheme hook!
  • Return what you need: You can return arrays (like useState) or objects (like our useStopwatch). Objects are usually better when you have more than two return values!

Final Thoughts 🏁

Custom hooks turn you from a “coder” into an “architect.” They make your components purely about the look (UI), while your hooks handle the brain (Logic).

Next time you find yourself writing a useEffect that looks familiar, ask yourself: "Should this be a Custom Hook?" The answer is usually a resounding YES.

Happy coding! 🚀

Best,

Komal

items.title: Solving the Multi-Session Problem: Making Multiple Apps Coexist on the Same Server
items.author: komal shehzadi
items.description:
Ever logged into one app… only to find yourself mysteriously logged out of another running on the same server?
Yeah — that’s the multi-session problem, and it happens more often than you think.

When you deploy multiple web apps (say, frontend portals, admin panels, or analytics dashboards) on the same domain or subdomain, they often end up sharing browser storage — localStorage, cookies, or sessionStorage.
That means one app’s login state can overwrite another’s, breaking sessions and confusing users.

In this post, I’ll walk you through what causes it, how I fixed it, and how you can make your own apps multi-session friendly 🔧

💥 The Problem

Let’s say you have two Angular or React apps deployed on the same server:

  • https://portal.company.com
  • https://admin.company.com

Or even two apps hosted under the same domain path:

  • https://company.com/app1
  • https://company.com/app2

Both apps use browser storage (like localStorage) to store authentication tokens.

If both use a common key like:

localStorage.setItem("ACCESS_TOKEN", token);

Guess what happens?
When you log into App1, it sets the ACCESS_TOKEN.
When you log into App2, it overwrites that same key.
Now both apps start reading each other’s tokens — resulting in random logouts, broken authentication, and 401 errors everywhere.

🎯 The Goal

The goal is to make each app maintain its own isolated session, even if they share the same server and domain.

That means:

  • Each app stores its token and config data separately.
  • Sessions remain independent.
  • Logging into one app won’t affect the other.

🧩 The Fix — Scoped Storage Keys

The simplest and cleanest way to solve this is by namespacing your storage keys.

Instead of:

ACCESS_TOKEN
USER_DATA
APP_CONFIG

You give each app its own prefix or environment tag, like:

APP1_ACCESS_TOKEN
APP2_ACCESS_TOKEN

This can be automated using an environment variable.

Example: local-storage.service.ts

@Injectable({ providedIn: 'root' })
export class LocalStorageService {
  private prefix = (window as any).__env?.appPrefix || 'APP1_';

saveData(key: string, data: any) {
    localStorage.setItem(this.prefix + key, JSON.stringify(data));
  }

getDataObject<T>(key: string): T | null {
    const data = localStorage.getItem(this.prefix + key);
    return data ? JSON.parse(data) as T : null;
  }

deleteData(key: string) {
    localStorage.removeItem(this.prefix + key);
  }
}

Now each app has its own localStorage namespace — simple, elegant, and effective.

⚙️ Environment-Based Config Files

To make this dynamic across environments (e.g. dev, uat, prod),
you can load an external config file like dev.local.config.json or prod.config.json on app startup.

{
  "appPrefix": "PORTAL_",
  "apiUrl": "https://api.company.com/portal/"
}

Then in main.ts:

fetch('/assets/config/dev.local.config.json')
  .then(res => res.json())
  .then(config => {
    (window as any).__env = config;
    platformBrowserDynamic().bootstrapModule(AppModule);
  });

That way, each app automatically loads the right config and prefix depending on where it’s deployed.

🔐 Bonus Tip: Scoped Cookies or SessionStorage

If your backend uses cookies for tokens instead of localStorage,
you can still isolate sessions by setting different cookie paths or subdomains.

For example:

Set-Cookie: token=xyz; Path=/app1; Secure; HttpOnly;

and

Set-Cookie: token=abc; Path=/app2; Secure; HttpOnly;

That ensures browsers won’t mix cookies between apps.

🚀 Result

After implementing this approach, I could:

  • Log into multiple apps hosted on the same server without conflicts.
  • Use environment-specific configs for clean separation.
  • Stop unexpected 401s and logout loops entirely.

It’s a simple improvement, but it completely changes the developer and user experience.

💡 Takeaway

Multi-session support isn’t just about authentication — it’s about making your app environment-aware and future-proof.

🧩 Every app should know who it is, where it lives, and where its data belongs.

Whether you’re deploying Angular, React, or any SPA framework — always give your app its own identity through namespaced storage and config-driven environments.

Have you faced weird logout issues between apps on the same domain?
Try this fix and say goodbye to session collisions forever 😎

Best,

Komal Shehzadi
